“Now,” said Mr. Lorry, after they had both been silent a moment, gently resting his hand on the Doctor's arm again, “what do you think caused this attack?”

“I believe,” Doctor Manette replied, “that the thoughts and memories which first caused his illness returned with unusual force. Certain deeply painful connections were brought vividly back to him, I think. He had probably been afraid for a long time that these memories would return—under particular circumstances, perhaps, or on some particular occasion. He tried to prepare himself, but couldn't. Perhaps that very effort left him less able to bear it.”

“Would he remember what happened during the relapse?” Mr. Lorry asked, with understandable hesitation.

The Doctor looked hopelessly around the room, shook his head, and answered quietly, “Nothing at all.”

“Now, about the future,” Mr. Lorry suggested.

“About the future,” the Doctor said, regaining his steady voice, “I would be very hopeful. Since Heaven mercifully allowed him to recover so soon, I would have great hope. He gave way under the pressure of something complicated that he had long feared, partly foreseen, and struggled against. Since he recovered after that storm broke and passed, I would hope the worst was over.”

“Well, well! That's a great comfort. I am thankful!” said Mr. Lorry.

“I am thankful!” the Doctor repeated, bowing his head reverently.

“There are two other things,” Mr. Lorry said, “that I'm anxious to understand. May I go on?”

“You could do your friend no greater kindness.” The Doctor offered him his hand.

“The first, then. He spends much time studying and has exceptional energy. He devotes himself eagerly to learning more about his profession, carrying out experiments, and many other things. Does he do too much?”

“I don't think so. His mind may have an unusually strong need to stay busy. That may be partly his natural character and partly a result of his suffering. The less he occupied himself with healthy interests, the more danger there would be of his thoughts turning in an unhealthy direction. He may have watched himself and discovered this.”

“You're sure he isn't putting himself under too much strain?”

“I think I'm quite sure.”

“My dear Manette, if he were overworking himself now—”

“My dear Lorry, I doubt that could easily happen. His mind has been pulled violently in one direction, and it needs something to balance that pull.”

“Forgive my persistence; I'm a businessman. Suppose for a moment that he was overworking himself. Would that show itself in another return of this illness?”

“‘We called at your residence,’ said the first, ‘and, having failed to find you at home, were told that you had probably walked this way. We followed in the hope of catching you. Will you kindly get into the carriage?’

“Both spoke and carried themselves imperiously, and as these words were uttered they moved to enclose me between themselves and the carriage door. They carried weapons. I carried none.

“‘Gentlemen,’ I said, ‘forgive me; but it is my custom to ask who honours me by requesting my services, and the nature of the case to which I am called.’

“The man who had spoken second answered this. ‘Doctor, those who require you are persons of rank. Concerning the nature of the case, our faith in your abilities assures us that you will discover it yourself more accurately than we could explain it. Enough. Will you kindly get into the carriage?’

“I had no choice but to obey, and entered without a word. Both followed me, the last leaping in after he had raised the steps. The carriage turned and continued at its previous pace.

“I give this conversation precisely as it happened. I do not doubt that every word is the same. I recount all things exactly as they occurred, forcing my thoughts not to stray from the work. At the broken marks which follow, I stop for the present and return the paper to its place of concealment.

“The carriage passed out of the streets, through the North Barrier, and onto the country road. Two-thirds of a league beyond the Barrier—a distance I measured not then, but afterwards when I travelled it—it turned off the main avenue and soon halted at an isolated house. All three of us descended and followed a soft, wet path across a garden, where an untended fountain had overflowed, to the house door. The bell was not answered at once, and one of my two escorts struck the man who opened the door across the face with his heavy riding-glove.

“There was nothing in the deed particularly to catch my notice, for I had seen ordinary people beaten more often than dogs. But the other gentleman, equally angry, dealt the man a similar blow with his arm; and the brothers' appearance and manner were then so precisely alike that I perceived for the first time that they were twins.

“Since we had stepped down at the outer gate, which was locked, and which one brother unlocked to let us through and locked again, I had heard cries coming from a room upstairs.

All this, and much, much more, I would gladly describe in detail. But to speak plainly, I must receive my reward. I long to return to my family and my home. As the price of any further information I provide—and in view of the light I can shed on many highly important areas of physical and metaphysical science—I must ask your honorable body to use its influence to secure my pardon for the crime I committed in causing the deaths of the creditors when I left Rotterdam. That, then, is the purpose of this document. Its bearer, an inhabitant of the moon whom I have persuaded and suitably instructed to act as my messenger to earth, will await your Excellencies' decision and bring me the pardon, if there is any way to obtain it.

“I have the honor to remain, etc., your Excellencies' most humble servant,

“HANS PFAALL.”

When this remarkable document had been read, Professor Rub-a-dub reportedly dropped his pipe to the ground in utter amazement. Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk removed his spectacles, polished them, and put them in his pocket; then, forgetting himself and his dignity altogether, he spun around three times on his heel in a supreme display of wonder and admiration. There could be no question: the pardon must be secured. At least, Professor Rub-a-dub swore a hearty oath to that effect, and the illustrious Von Underduk eventually agreed. Taking his fellow scientist's arm, he set off home without a word, as quickly as possible, to consider what steps should be taken. At the door of the burgomaster's house, however, the professor ventured to point out that the messenger had chosen to disappear—no doubt terrified by the ferocious appearance of Rotterdam's citizens. A pardon would therefore serve little purpose, since nobody but a man from the moon would attempt a journey over such an enormous distance. The burgomaster acknowledged the truth of this observation, and the matter ended there. Rumor and speculation, however, did not. Once published, the letter prompted all kinds of gossip and opinion. Some people who considered themselves especially wise even made themselves absurd by denouncing the whole affair as nothing more than a hoax. But with people of that sort, I believe, “hoax” is a general name for anything beyond their understanding. Personally, I cannot imagine what evidence supports their accusation. Let us examine what they have to say:
